In rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I first want to congratulate the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply for their contributions. They both did exceedingly well. I realize, however, that the speech from the throne was not of their making. In my opinion there is nothing in the speech from the throne to correct the ills that beset us in this country where we have so many natural resources. Traditionally, these hon. members made reference to their own constituencies and this was very interesting. I should like to follow their example and make some reference to my own constituency of Welland.
We have fine people living in the constituency of Welland. Anglo-Saxon people comprise the majority of our population, but during the last generation or so we have had a great influx of French-speaking Canadians as well as people from southern and western Europe. These people live in complete harmony, and they and their descendants are making a fine contribution to our Canadian

way of life. There is no other part of Canada that I would rather represent than the constituency of Welland.
Our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) graced Welland with a visit last March during his election tour. No one took the trouble to invite me to that meeting but I learned what occurred there. I can assure the Prime Minister that if he will come back now, he will have an even larger meeting. Some of the people who attended the last meeting said they would provide him with a theme song, "Oh, Promise Me". The meeting the Prime Minister held in Welland was, in part at least, composed of a captive audience because school children were brought in by the bus load from schools in the surrounding school areas. Then, too, many people arrived at the meeting at no cost to themselves because a canvass had been made and car drivers were paid $5 and $10 to deliver loads of people to that meeting.
There were many people, however, who attended the meeting without any urging. I refer now to the unemployed and the fruit and vegetable growers. What they heard from the Prime Minister in the way of promises must have been music to their ears. According to the press, he promised the unemployed that no one would suffer as a result of unemployment as long as he was Prime Minister of Canada. He went even further than that, and this was afterwards echoed on television by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) when he said that the unemployment would be pretty well cleared up by mid-summer. Mid-summer has come and gone and many of these same men and women are still unemployed. Their numbers have greatly increased in the Welland area.
At the time of the June election when this government came into power, we had comparatively few unemployed. When the Prime Minister was in Welland the number stood at about 2,400. Today it is difficult to ascertain the exact number. I am told it is in the neighbourhood of 4,000. These figures used to be published, but they are not published any longer. The reeve of one municipality told me that the relief rolls were up by about 400 per cent over those of a year ago. In the practice of medicine I meet and treat many of the unemployed. I know that they want work and not the dole. Many of them have purchased homes, furniture and the other necessities of life. They have had to go into debt and they cannot meet their obligations. Surely this government should soon realize that it does not help the peace of mind of the unemployed to be told that while unemployment is greater this winter it is not increasing as greatly percentage-wise. Last night I believe the Minister of Finance, speaking in the Chateau
The Address-Mr. McMillan Laurier, used the word "proportion", and said that the proportion of increase of unemployed was not as great.
When a man is out of work, just getting a mere subsistance for himself and his family, these vague percentage quotations by the government do nothing to lighten his burden. I feel heartily sorry for the unemployed and our government is doing nothing to provide work for the younger people coming into the labour market. The new federal-provincial scheme to help municipalities provide work for the unemployed by helping to provide new projects for the municipalities is of little use. It is too little and too late.
The St. Catharines Standard for example, a few days ago had an article which said that not one man hour of work had been provided in that city for the unemployed by this scheme. Also, I have a letter here from the city of Welland claiming that the help provided under this scheme is too restricted. This was written to me by the city clerk of Welland, and he says that the council and corporation of Welland at its meeting on January 6, 1959, viewed with alarm the narrow limits of unemployment assistance and work projects available to the smaller cities in the province of Ontario. I know that this scheme is of little help in the towns and smaller cities. I am not familiar with how the scheme might work out in the larger cities, but I fail to see that it can be of any great help, particularly since I have seen the figure given out by the Department of Labour. Canada cannot afford to have so many people unemployed and non-productive. There is nothing which breaks the spirit and morale of a person more than idleness. Canadians deserve the right to work.
At the meeting in Welland the Prime Minister also dwelt on the poor returns received by fruit and vegetable growers for their products. I agree with the Prime Minister that they should have had a greater share of the national income. But what has happened since this government came to power? Many of these fruit and vegetable growers tell me that their costs have risen and their returns for 1958 in respect of their crops have been the worse since before the war. The Prime Minister made a very emotional appeal. There was a fine old lady at that meeting who came from a farm community. She wept because she said she had never heard a man speak with such sympathy for the farmers as did the Prime Minister that day. The price of asparagus was very much to the fore.
Spring was coming on, and these producers were very much concerned about the price. In the year before, under the Liberal government, the price had fallen from 23 cents

The Address-Mr. McMillan to 22 cents and in some cases to 21-|- cents. Now what has happened? The present government set the floor at 18 cents under which they placed a three cent deficiency payment, and asparagus has never since that time sold above 15 cents in Ontario and 14 cents in British Columbia. In the province of Ontario the government paid a deficiency payment of three cents a pound so that the producer in Ontario got 18 cents and the producer in British Columbia received 17 cents.
As for peaches, the floor price was set at $83 a ton which is the lowest price received by the peach growers for grade A peaches since before the war. I understand that the government has not yet settled with the growers for this year. We understand that cherries could not be all sold and that much of the crop rotted on the trees. The cold storage plants took all they could but according to the last information I received before Christmas the farmers had not been paid for this fruit put into cold storage. There is one big chain store in the Niagara district which was selling American table corn when our corn was ripe. You could stand in the store and look out the window and see the farmers harvesting their corn in the adjoining fields.
I think that our unemployment and our depressed economy are in a considerable part due to the trade and fiscal policies of this government. I will give some examples of each. Hon. members will recall that in June of 1957 our economy was good. In fact, it was so good that the Prime Minister said he could divert 15 per cent of trade from the United States to Great Britain. Hon. members will also recall that about the same time, or shortly afterwards, the United States accommodated the Prime Minister by cutting off 15 per cent of our oil imports into the northwestern United States. Then, in December of 1957, this government sent a buying mission to Britain; they were to buy and not to sell Canadian products and this was done at a time when unemployment in Britain was very low and when in Canada we had plenty. We got a report from that buying mission. This report was printed in Toronto and not by the queen's printer. Oddly enough, that report refers to nothing that was bought. It reads something like the social column of a woman's page in a newspaper. It says whom the delegation visited, by whom they were received, how they were entertained, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) joined the group, when he left it and when he rejoined it.
The only inkling I received that a big trade switch was on was in a Port Colborne newspaper. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was there, according to the paper,

and he announced that the government intended to switch even more trade from the United States to Britain than it had already done. I can thank the hon. minister for helping to elect me because by that time our unemployment in the Welland area had increased from practically nothing to about 2,400. I argued that if the big switch had helped produce that many it was surely time to call a halt to that type of cause of unemployment.
This evening I heard the minister refer to the fact that we would in time see the long term result of this attempt to switch trade to Britain. I do not know anything about the long term result; I am giving one of the short term results. I have always been greatly interested in Canada's effort to promote trade with Britain. Since our trade with the United States has been cut by about 15 per cent I wondered why our trade with Britain had not been increased. Following our buying mission to Britain, however, our imports went down by 7.6 per cent in the third quarter of 1958 and by about 1 per cent for the first nine months of 1958.
It appears to me that before our government meets in conference with the United States or even with members of the commonwealth it always seems to give them a slap in the face first. We all recall the first conference of our four ministers with their opposite numbers in the United States when secretary of commerce, Sinclair Weeks, said to reporters: "we fixed them." I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) got another explanation to mean that he meant: "We fixed them up". But the newspaper accounts, even in the Toronto Globe and Mail at that time talked about the brush-off our ministers received in Washington.
The United States is our best customer, and living along the border as I do I have an opportunity to see many of the Buffalo and Niagara Falls newspapers, among others, which circulate in our area. I have had the opportunity to read them over the years. Some have said quite openly that if the Canadian Prime Minister and his followers acted as some of them were talking, the election foreboded a difficult period in trade and other relations between the United States and Canada. One paper in my area-a paper that supports this government-went so far as to say it would not be surprised if incidents occurred between Canadians and Americans living in the Niagara district.
The United States press referred to the diversion of trade proposed by this government and later on in one or two dispatches from Ottawa it was stated that Canadian raw

materials such as iron ore would be processed in Canadian plants and not shipped south of the border to give jobs to people in the United States. I think it is fine to process all the raw materials we can but I could not conceive of a worse preparation for a conference with our United States friends.
How about the commonwealth conference itself? We have had two of them, first the Mont Tremblant conference and latterly the Montreal conference. The preparation for the Montreal conference involved an added tariff, as hon. members will recall, placed on British woollens, a procedure of this government that certainly did not go unnoticed by the British government.
I have in my hand a copy of Hansard, of the British House of Commons of December 2, 1958 when the government of that country debated commonwealth affairs and I shall quote extracts from the speeches of a Conservative member, a Labour member and a Liberal member. I should like to ask some of the members of the Conservative party in this house to read what Sir Albert Braith-waite said about the Montreal conference. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) said that the commonwealth conference was unique. We shall see how unique it was. These are the remarks of Sir Albert Braithwaite the Conservative member for Harrow West:
First of all, I should like to pay tribute to the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the president of the board of trade for the brilliance which they displayed in leading our own delegation to the Montreal conference. Reading between the lines, it seems to me that what they did there literally saved the conference from being almost a stalemate. They infused some life into it. At the same time I am not satisfied that the conference report is by any means a document upon which to rebuild and revitalize the British commonwealth of nations. Its implications are narrow. It is phlegmatic. It is not precise enough in its conclusions, and it gives no real, positive direction on how even those conclusions will be carried out.
I wanted something much more vital to lead our commonwealth affairs than a lot of pious platitudes. Many people have said a great many things about how we should develop the commonwealth but there has been a remarkable absence of action since the Montreal conference took place. The Canadian Prime Minister came over here and made great speeches on what should be done, but I have seen no real reflection in deeds implementing the words which he uttered.

Yet what has happened? Only this summer Mr. Diefenbaker's government actually raised their tariff

Here is an essential British export to a dollar market, produced by one of our most important industries, which at the moment is acutely depressed, and yet Mr. Diefenbaker, who professes, I am sure sincerely, to have great enthusiasm for Anglo-Canadian trade, raises the tariff against British woollen goods just before the conference.

The government appears to be advancing backwards by stealth.

It put me in mind of the time Winston Churchill was in New York and was asked what he thought of the Attlee government. He replied that when he was out of his country he never criticized his government but when he was home he never left off criticizing it. Surely, this great Conservative leader of all time, Winston Churchill, has by example long since shown us the way to keep our Canadian family affairs at home and the Leader of the Opposition has done just that. For doing so, however, he has suffered unfair criticism and ridicule from our Prime Minister.
I hold in my hand an editorial from the December 31 issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail. I wish to read two sentences from it. The heading of the editorial is, "Twelve Months of Mystery", and reads in part as follows:
In his New Year's message to the Canadian people, Liberal Leader Pearson refers to the "distressing dilemma" of rising prices and inflationary pressures 66968-9-12
The Address-Miss Aitken in a period of recession and unemployment. Dilemma, irony, anomaly, farce or tragedy, mare's nest or monkey puzzle-one might call it a great many things.
Let us call a halt to this monkey business in finance. We do not want to sink into another mess like the conversion loan.
Last year the Minister of Finance said that this government did not need to take advice from anyone, and he emphasized this by saying, "let there be no question about that".
I used to listen to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I am sorry he is not in his seat. He was the opposition financial critic of the former government. I could not always agree with him, yet I thought he spoke responsibly and his views on finance were, in my mind, sounder than anything displayed by anyone so far in this government. I cannot help but express to this house the secret hope that the Minister of Finance would consult him for direction. I feel that if he had done so from the start he would not be in the financial mess in which he finds himself today.
I would like to quote one last paragraph from this Globe and Mail editorial "Twelve Months of Mystery". Perhaps it should read, "Mystery of Life Under the Tory Government." However, in the last paragraph of this editorial in the Globe and Mail I find the following:
As we say, a peculiar year; a year in which our economy found itself very much out of balance, if not indeed out of control. Sweeping changes are obviously in order from top to bottom of our economic life; and this will require strong leadership. We have a right to expect, and demand, such leadership during 1959 from those in a position to provide it.
I hope the government can provide it.

Mr. Speaker, before embarking on a few comments I should like to add my voice to the congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Like previous speakers, I was very impressed with the speeches that the hon. member for Pro-vencher and the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet made, and I congratulate them.
I was surprised, Mr. Speaker, and continue to be surprised that we should have heard so much gloom, doom and criticism from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and now from his followers. I was surprised because it is quite obvious that he is still far removed from the grass roots in the country. You will remember that when he became leader of the party he said that it was time

The Address-Miss Aitken that the Liberals got away from the brass and back to the grass. I was surprised to hear all this gloom and doom because, as I think most of us will agree, one would have thought that after our four-month recess the Leader of the Opposition would have a better idea of what the people of Canada, the grass roots, are really thinking.
Personally, I am extremely gratified at the political consciousness of the people, certainly those in my constituency of York-Humber, and I am grateful for their awareness of the problems that face us all in Canada. I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has played a major role in sparking the interest of the people in our national welfare. He has the great gift of getting close to the people, of inspiring belief

in him and in his honesty, courage and deep sense of responsibility.
On the other hand, nothing will convince me that the Leader of the Opposition, in his pitiful pessimism, is speaking for the people of Canada, the grass roots of Canada. He may have been speaking for the sadly decimated Liberal party but certainly not for the people of Canada. There are three or four items I should like to speak about with reference to the speech from the throne. Shall I go ahead or shall I call it six o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement with regard to the United Nations wheat conference, the second session of which will be convened at Geneva on January 27, and Canada will be represented there by a strong delegation.
The first session was held at Geneva from October 28 to November 7, 1958, and was attended by 41 countries as members and 9 as observers. speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):

subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON APPLICATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AIR LINES
speechtext:
I should like now, Mr. Speaker, to table in English and in French copies of the report of the air transport board to the Minister of Transport on the need for additional transcontinental air services in Canada, and on the application of Canadian Pacific Air Lines for a licence to operate a scheduled service serving Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary, Saskatoon, Regina, Winnipeg, Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal.
The investigation of the board and its hearing of the Canadian Pacific Air Lines application was dealt with in regional hearings in Vancouver, Edmonton, Regina, Winnipeg and Moncton between October 6 and October 15, 1958, and in final hearings commencing October 20 and terminating December 3, 1958, in Ottawa; and involved consideration of several dozen briefs and well over a thousand pages of oral evidence.
The board found that additional transcontinental air services could not be introduced at this time without major detrimental effect to existing operations, and without economic hardships and possible disadvantages for scheduled air lines, including the applicant. The board found that the application of Canadian Pacific Air Lines should be denied because its expense estimates were computed on an unreasonable added cost basis, with no projection on a fully allocated cost basis; its revenues were estimated without any traffic study; and the schedules for its proposed service appeared to have been based on optimistic block speeds.
However, the board also found that the position of Canadian Pacific Air Lines as an international air carrier needed strengthening, and it has recommended issuing to Canadian Pacific Air Lines a licence to operate a domestic scheduled service from Vancouver to Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal, to connect Canadian Pacific Air Lines' existing international operations. This new service would be limited to one return flight a day, on which domestic as well as international passengers could be carried. It recommended that the adequacy of this arrangement be reviewed again in two years to see whether additional services would then be warranted. The board also recommended that where limited controlled competition would result

Tabling of Notes
in improving the position of regional air carriers, this be authorized, and has indicated that it feels it should make an intensive investigation of the position of regional air carriers in this connection.
I have informed the air transport board that I am prepared to accept their findings in regard to the foregoing.
The board has also recommended that a substantial portion of the government work now being performed by the R.C.A.F. be diverted to commercial air carriers. There is, of course, an obvious requirement that the Department of National Defence maintain a military air transport organization in being. At the same time, military authorities have always recognized their interest in maintaining civil air transport services which can assist them in time of emergency and, indeed, much of the present work of the larger regional air carriers in Canada is in the direct supply of military installations in the north. This particular recommendation of the air transport board will require further careful examination and I propose to consult with my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, about it.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) requested on Friday last that the two notes received from the United States-the notes of June 26, 1958 and September 3, 1958- and our reply of October 24, 1958 be tabled. I desire to table those documents now. These notes will, I believe, warrant careful
EMr. Hees.]
reading by hon. members, as they provide a detailed exposition of the views of the United States government and of the views of the Canadian government on these matters.
In the United States note No. 284 of June 26, 1958, written and presented to us after a general reference to amendments to the Customs Act by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech of June 17, 1958, the ambassador of the United States drew our attention to the main point on which his government saw cause for concern. The note of June 26 was not a protest; in effect it requested that the Canadian government should not introduce any provisions in the amendments to the Customs Act which would be contrary to our international obligations under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. We gave due weight to the observations of the United States while the proposed legislation was being prepared, and we drafted a bill that does not contravene the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
The note dated June 26, 1958 was delivered on June 30, 1958, and it was forthwith brought to the attention of the Department of Finance, the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of National Revenue; copies with comments were circulated to them and to the Department of Agriculture on July 16, 1958. The note dated and delivered on September 3 was circulated to the departments concerned on September 8. I now table these notes.

speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I advised the hon. member for Laurier that I would make a further statement as soon as I received it from the management of Canadian National Railways regarding his request that the railway be asked to delay the diversionary work on Victoria bridge until the construction of Champlain bridge had been completed. The management have now given me the following statement.
The Victoria bridge is considered the most important railway transportation link in Canada. Across it passes well over a half million railway cars a year carrying commerce valued at about $2 billion and constituting by far the greater part of the traffic to and from eastern Quebec, the maritime provinces and the United States. It is necessary, therefore, that co-ordination between the Victoria bridge and the St. Lawrence seaway should be such as to present a minimum of delay, since the consequences of any interruption of this huge traffic flow would be incalculable.
Inquiries of the Ministry
With the construction of the seaway project it was necessary to arrange for the opening of the bridge to permit passage of vessels through the canals. A simple lift span would have a disastrous effect on railway and highway traffic. It was therefore considered necessary to construct a rail and highway diversion for the purpose of providing an alternative route for rail and highway traffic when the lift span is in operation at the St. Lambert lock. The co-ordination of Victoria bridge with the navigation channel has constituted a most complex problem, but the management is satisfied that the method of co-ordination finally evolved embodies the best possible solution under all the circumstances, in that it will achieve a complete separation of all types of traffic-marine, rail, and highway-without interruption to any one of them.
There was a dispute between the seaway and the railway as to which ought to bear the cost of the diversion and related facilities. This dispute was temporarily resolved by the terms of an agreement executed between the seaway authority and Canadian National Railways dated January 12, 1956, when the hon. member was president of the seaway, under which Canadian National Railways undertook to construct a diversionary bridge and to complete it, as far as practicable, concurrently with the construction of the lift span at the St. Lambert lock. There was a further understanding between the seaway and Canadian National Railways that it was vital for railway traffic to have uninterrupted movement, and that until the diversionary bridge made this possible the railway is to have control of the opening and closing of the lift span. Consequently shipping in the canal may be seriously delayed until the diversionary bridge is ready for use. The urgency for completion of the rail diversion is, therefore, definitely related to the needs of navigation, since any interruption of movement will affect shipping and not the railway.
Following construction of the diversion and related facilities, the responsibility for payment of the costs involved will be determined by the governor in council.

subtopic: EFFECT ON CANADIAN EXPORTS OF U.S. BRUCELLOSIS CONTROL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EFFECT ON CANADIAN EXPORTS OF U.S. BRUCELLOSIS CONTROL
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Speaker. Has the minister seen the statement in today's Globe and Mail that exports of cattle from Canada to the United States will be seriously curtailed by the new United States brucellosis control program, and will he inform the house what effect this program will have on exports from this country to the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: EFFECT ON CANADIAN EXPORTS OF U.S. BRUCELLOSIS CONTROL
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have seen it. I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. I think it is desirable that X should make a statement in connection with the matter so that fears on the part of cattlemen which this and similar reports are likely to have aroused should be set at rest.
The implication in recent press reports that exports of cattle from Ontario will be limited mainly to the counties of Oxford and Prince Edward is misleading. On November 8, 1958 the United States introduced new cattle import certification requirements for brucellosis disease. These new regulations permit the entry into the United States of six classes of cattle:
1.	Cattle from brucellosis-free listed herds.
2.	Cattle from brucellosis-certified areas.
3.	Cattle from herds which are neither listed nor in certified areas but which have passed a negative herd test within 90 days.
4.	Cattle up to 30 months of age, officially calfhood-vaccinated against brucellosis.
5.	Range cattle of the beef breeds from western Canada.
6.	Cattle for immediate slaughter.
There are in Canada approximately 5,000 herds under the brucellosis-free listed herd policy. Cattle from all these herds are eligible for export. In Ontario two counties, Oxford and Prince Edward, are already certified areas. Three other counties, namely Halton, Stormont and Dundas, will be certified within the next few days. Nine other

counties are under test, all of which should be completed before summer. In the meantime, as herds in these counties or elsewhere pass a negative test they are eligible for export. These 14 counties include most of the major Ontario cattle export areas. A further 17 Ontario counties have been accepted for testing and will be proceeded with as quickly as possible.
Elsewhere in Canada, the province of Prince Edward Island has been completely certified. Three counties have been certified in Nova Scotia and five in New Brunswick, and three additional counties are under test in each of those provinces. Seven areas are under test in Quebec, although none has been certified to date. Testing is proceeding in western Canada, and some areas have been certified.
As a result of the progress in brucellosis testing and the provision for the export of western feeder cattle and cattle for immediate slaughter, the new United States requirements should not seriously restrict Canadian cattle exports. As I stated at the beginning, I hope this statement will set at rest the fears which have been communicated to me from several quarters that our exports of cattle to the United States are going to be seriously curtailed.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. H. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was speaking of one of the problems affecting unemployment, and I stated that the problem is how to produce without pricing ourselves not only out of our own market but out of the markets of the world. I indicated that employment depends on trade and the ability to sell our services and products at competitive prices in Canada and abroad.
As I understand it there are several industries across Canada today, particularly the clothing and garment industry and some parts of the electrical industry, that must consider moving their factories from Canada because they cannot compete even in Canada or meet competition from outside countries such as Japan. Another factor contributing to unemployment has been the result of disputes between management and labour sometimes resulting in strikes. In a democratic system we must rely on the responsibility of the leaders of both management and labour to settle these disputes without government dictation, and I hope the leaders on both sides will consider the over-all effect of these actions. These are not decisions for government but rather for labour and management. Many of these problems cannot be solved entirely by legislation, subsidies, tariffs or artificial stimulants. These problems require co-operation of all the people concerned.
May I make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that I do not say these things because I believe we are now in a disastrous or perilous situation, but rather because I am concerned that perhaps we might be pressured in the wrong direction, and I am voicing my concern before it is too late.
It has been a platform of our party, and I think it is the hope of every hon. member in this house, that we in this country will be able to develop our resources for the benefit of our people and to provide for a larger population. But if we price ourselves out of the markets of the world and even

out of our own markets we shall become little more than the distributors of our own raw materials, and history will record us as a nation not worthy of its heritage. I therefore suggest, in view of the importance of this to our future, that the government consider convening a national conference on unemployment and related subjects the membership of which might be composed of representatives of the three levels of government, of industry, labour, agriculture and economics, in the hope that we might solve this problem by a comprehensive and co-operative plan rather than spending time in this house hurling abuse across the floor as to who is the cause of the problem of unemployment.
Another area in which I believe we as a democratic nation are not measuring up to the competition which is being offered by the communist nations and satellites is the field of education. The implications of the scientific achievements of Russia are selfexplanatory. We can no longer pretend that we have a superior system; we must now prove it. We admit that in Canada we have no central body responsible for national leadership in this field. We must depend on the alertness of the ten provincial governments to co-operate in unison to meet the national need for high educational standards.
I commend the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Stinson) for bringing to our attention yesterday a study of our educational system as compared with those of East Germany and Russia. This report was prepared by Mr. Anthony Frisch, who was born of Austrian parents in Naples, Italy and studied science at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and McGill University. He came to Canada and during the war served with the R.C.A.F. Because of his knowledge of what has happened in Europe he became greatly concerned about the educational system in Canada. Through co-operation he obtained textbooks from Russia and Germany and from each Canadian province to use as the basis of his study. I think it is to his credit that he has given us this report so that it might be studied by educational authorities across Canada.
As was pointed out yesterday by the hon. member for York Centre, the study contains a table showing a break-down of related headings of subjects in the field of science such as mathematics, physics, chemistry and biology as taught in Canada, Russia and East Germany. This indicates that 71 headings are in use under the Russian system in the study of science, 13 being under mathematics, 19 under physics, 25 under chemistry and 14 under biology.
In comparing these subjects and relating them as closely as he could to equivalent

teaching in Canada he found that the province with the nearest approach to teaching the 71 subjects was Ontario with 54. In the matter of mathematics, where there were
13	units, the nearest province was Ontario with nine; in physics with 19 units the nearest province was Saskatchewan with 16; in chemistry with 25 units the nearest province was Ontario with 18; in biology with
14	units the nearest province was Quebec, the English section, with 14.
In respect of education in Ontario he made the following comments:
Mathematics
Ontario courses trail the soviet courses by about three years in the soviet equivalent grades 9 and 10. In the soviet equivalent grade 11. analytical calculus, as is the case with all other provinces, is not mentioned on the Ontario syllabus.
Physics
Ontario trails the soviet by two years in the soviet equivalent grade 9; one year in the soviet equivalent grade 10: one to two years in the first part of the soviet equivalent grade 11.
Chemistry
Ontario trails by three years the first two years of high schools; by two years the soviet equivalent grade 11; and does not touch at all the final soviet year, which is devoted exclusively to organic chemistry.
Biology
Grade 13 zoology and botany cover, however inadequately, the work of the soviet equivalent grades of nine, 10, 11 and 12.
He sets out in detail tables to back up his analogies. He came to the following conclusions:
1.	The soviet are able to teach their students, at an early age, to manipulate creatively abstract terms.
2.	At no time is subject matter repeated in subsequent grades.
3.	Subjects are not popularized to spoon-feed lower grades.
4.	Practical applications of laws and phenomena receive marginal treatments.
5.	Generally, we trail the soviet three years in mathematics and two years in science.
^he curricula of the 10 provinces show marked differences.
He makes the following suggestions for consideration:
Consequently, to ensure the survival and development of our talented children, most of whom survive despite the school system, it is suggested:
1.	That the federal government declare that there exists a state of emergency in education;
2.	That the federal government, through yearly I.Q. tests administered in consultation with the provinces, select the most talented students at the grade nine level, irrespective of geographic residence or academic performance;
3.	That these selected students be called "Canada scholars";
4.	That these students, provided they attend school and only that they pass their grade, be paid scholarships of the value of old age pensions through the welfare branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare but under no circumstances through the Canada Council as constituted at present;
The Address-Mr. Morton
5.	That the federal government, in consultation with the provinces, administer a further set of yearly I.Q. tests to all students at the grade 12 level;
6.	That the most talented of these students, provided only they pass their year, and irrespective of geographic residence, be called "Queen's scholars";
7.	That these students, as long as they attend a school or university, receive scholarships amounting to twice the amount of old age pensions.
Hon. members will note that he makes perhaps an indirect criticism of some of the teaching and methods of choosing our students on academic performance only because, in talking to me, he said that in some of our courses our students are taught to parrot back their knowledge rather than think on their own, and he felt that by emphasizing the intelligence side you would get a more independent type of student.
We may not all agree with the conclusions that he has brought before us, Mr. Speaker; we may not feel that the Russian system is perhaps as advanced as it is made out to be. Perhaps the Russian system of schools is not distributed across the country to the same extent as ours may be but I do not think we can afford to ignore those comparisons. I am also informed by Mr. Frisch that, according to his study, the Russians compare favourably with us in the humanities.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that since we have no central body responsible under government for this leadership in education as such, this might be a task that might well be gone into by the Canadian education association across Canada, which represents the ministers and the educational heads of all the provinces. Because of their experience they could study this problem and perhaps give us some leadership in the country in this respect. I think it is most important that we take those warnings now before it is too late.
We all look back at our history and we sort of laugh at those who during the days before it was discovered that the world was round clung to the idea that the world was flat. Perhaps we are in the same situation today in our history with respect to education. Many of our concepts of education and of the universe are changing and we must accept the fact that as the explorers of old, together with the leading scientists, proved that the world was round. So because of explorations now being made into space and the demands and the problems of the future world are going to be such that our present system of education, regardless of how well it may have served us in the past, is not adequate to serve our future needs.
It would be interesting to know, Mr. Speaker, among the experts whom we have employed in our various industries and research centres how many are from other

The Address-Mr. Morton countries. How much have we had to rely on experts from other countries? It is not a bad thing. We welcome those who come from other countries and we welcome their knowledge. I am almost sure that in its present development our educational system has not produced all the experts we have needed. As a matter of fact

this is an aside-we were discussing the matter of the Arrow with the members of the union in Toronto last week and they made the comment that the staff they brought together came from all countries of the world and that it would be a shame if that staff had to be dispersed. The thing that caught my attention was that in order to build up the expert staff for that task it was necessary to draw on outside experts to get the efficient team that was required.
We cannot be too proud, we cannot be blind, Mr. Speaker. We must give the Russians credit for advancement in their education. Perhaps those advances are our ultimate hope. They will learn the wisdom of letting other nations live side by side, each maintaining its own system. There is already slight evidence that the educated in Russia are seeing the folly of the dogmatic and rigid concepts of communism. I only hope that our educational leaders will swallow their pride and give us constructive leadership in improving our educational system and that we in government will give leadership in providing the funds that may be necessary.
I understand that at the present time about 3.11 per cent of personal income is being spent on education and that about 10 per cent of all the money spent on government affairs is spent on education. I should like to urge again that a select committee of the house be set up to study the financial needs of education in Canada. It is a problem that we must face. I think it is time to forget our regional prejudices and think as Canadians in developing educational systems across Canada in accordance with the needs of the provinces and of our growing nation. We should study how the central government can help financially without interfering with the rights of the provinces.
I again urge the Canadian educational association to undertake the sponsorship of a research program as to the future requirements of our country. I also urge the extension of the scholarships now provided. In the brief of the Canadian teachers' federation to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) last year the following statement is made and I think that we should bear it in mind.
The full development of this country economically, culturally, socially, and spiritually demands the full development of the potentialities of its youth. The extent of education of a Canadian boy or girl should

depend upon his or her ability to benefit by further education and not upon geographical location and the parent's pocketbook. Whether or not one concedes that a full education is the birthright of every citizen, there surely can be no doubt that the best interests of the nation require that every citizen be educated to the fullest extent of his capabilities.
I trust that we as Canadians, while proud of our resources, will recognize our destiny and combine in a constructive effort within our nation and with our friends to prove to the world that our system is better than that of the communists and that it gives greater hope to the individual.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in this debate. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), in a remarkable speech on Monday, brought to the attention of the house the inadequacies of the policies of the government in practically every field. He also chastised the government for its indecision, for its confusion and for its fumbling. I should like to limit myself this afternoon to one or two heads of government policy which to my mind are responsible in no small measure for the disastrous condition in which the country finds itself today.
Before proceeding, however, I should like to follow the tradition of the house from time immemorial and extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin), who discharged in excellent fashion the tasks of moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I want to refer particularly to that part of the speech of the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet which dealt with national unity. It has always been the doctrine of the Liberal party and all its leaders to uphold national unity in the house and throughout the country.
I should now like to refer to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had to say on Monday when he stated that the speech delivered by the Leader of the Opposition was not in keeping with his responsibilities. This to my mind was unfair criticism and I should like to tell the Prime Minister today that that part of his speech was not in keeping with his responsibilities as Prime Minister. The particular inference that he tried to leave that the criticisms of the Leader of the Opposition were similar to those made by communist leaders and especially Mr. Mikoyan is certainly not in keeping with the kind of leadership that the Canadian people have the right to expect at this moment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There was no such
implication.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
After having made that
reference to Mr. Mikoyan, the Prime Minister went on to say, as found on page 53 of Hansard for January 19:
When one considers the difficulties confronting the free world in terms of an economic attack one must conclude this is not the time for the kind of speech that was delivered here this afternoon with such relish.
What were the points made by the Leader of the Opposition with reference to the economic situation? He outlined the unemployment problems in the country in realistic terms, at all times basing his argument upon figures taken from government statistics. On that basis he criticized the inadequacy of government policy and he urged the Prime Minister to take new steps to deal with this very serious social evil. My leader was in very good company indeed when he made these statements because, the archbishop of Montreal, Cardinal Leger, dealt with this problem on at least two occasions. Here is what he had to say.
(Translation):

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not in the same sense. (Text):

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I hear someone say, "not in the same sense." Just let him listen to this. On September 18, 1958 the cardinal spoke to the delegates at the annual meeting of the federation of Catholic workers of Canada and, as reported by La Presse of Montreal, here is what he had to say:
His Eminence deplored that hundreds of thousands of workers are without work in a country immensely rich and in full development. "We cannot hide the anxieties that are inspired in us by the considerable amount of unemployment which took place last winter and which unfortunately strikes today in the homes of many workers.
I should also like to read from the pastoral letter of the cardinal which was read to all his diocesans in the archdiocese of Montreal on Sunday, January 18. Cardinal Leger said:
A Christian cannot remain indifferent in a situation which creates such great suffering. Behind the statistics and figures we must discern the men and women, the children and the aged who are reduced to poverty and exposed to the terrible temptations of despair.
Then again:
A just and lasting solution to unemployment involves respect for man's natural right to work, encouragement of a high and stable level of employment and a more salutary direction for the economy.
Note these significant words.
The situation requires the intervention of government to take new and audacious steps.
I ask the house, is that so different from what was said by my leader when he asked the Prime Minister the other day and again today whether he would interrupt the speech from the throne in order to bring forward new measures to deal with unemployment.
The Address-Mr. Chevrier
I should like to discuss this question. In so doing I feel that I am in better company with the cardinal and with the Leader of the Opposition than I am with the government. But I am not alone with these two distinguished gentlemen, Mr. Speaker. Listen to what the hon. member for Prince Albert, now the Prime Minister, had to say in 1955 when he sat on this side of the house and when conditions were in no way comparable to the serious situation the country faces today and which year was the most prosperous of the 1950's. I quote from page 2034 of Hansard of March 15, 1955:
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said he very seriously regretted the developing unemployment across the country when he spoke in the house some weeks ago . . . they express solicitude. They mobilize statistics. But the Prime Minister, from whom the people of Canada want to hear, with the prestige of his position, remains silent in the face of a problem that wrings the hearts of the people.
The hon. member for Prince Albert went on to say this:
What a hopeless picture! The government, faced for the first time with serious unemployment . . . is unable to give any hope. We are unable to rouse them into placing before the people of Canada some of the picture.
Later on he said this:
We do not believe in preaching pessimism; we do not want to see the condition of affairs brought about which will create panic; but we are asking the government to act now-
Then dealing with the figures of the Canadian National Railways, which were then much better from the point of view of revenue than they are at the present time, here is what the hon. member for Prince Albert said:
Why not face that picture? Is it not a fact that some 10.000 men have been laid off? The railway-men ask: what is the picture for the future? After all, it is a government corporation and they have a right to expect information regarding the railway company owned by the dominion.
Then still further:
The municipalities are loaded down with unemployment relief . . . What is the attitude of the government?
Those are words which were used by the present Prime Minister when conditions were far better than they are today. Yet the Prime Minister dares to criticize the Leader of the Opposition because of the language which he used in his speech on Monday. I can only say:
(Translation):
Other times, other ways.
The Conservative government is starting the session on the wrong footing. Its finances are in poor shape. Over the whole fiscal year,

The Address-Mr. Chevrier the government's total deficit-including budgetary and non-budgetary items-will reach $1,600,000,000.
Where will we find the money to offset this deficit? Either by increasing taxes or by borrowing. As you know, the government decided to borrow by selling bonds. Everybody knows today that this financial policy of the government is causing a steady fall in the value of government bonds. In fact, last year in mid-December, $100 government bonds were down to $94.50.
At present, being less and less able to borrow from the public, the government is facing a financial crisis. But this is not the whole story, for the financial responsibilities of the government will cause a new increase of expenditures during the new fiscal period so that next year again the government will face another large deficit, unless it decides to increase taxes. Even if it should do so-and taxes are already high in Canada-its disastrous financial policy would nevertheless, this year, contribute to inflation and rising prices.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, prices are already on the way up, as official government statistics well show. Indeed the consumer's price index has gone up 3.5 per cent since 1957. The general wholesale price index shows that they have risen by two points in less than two months, that is last October and November, which means, as stated by the dominion bureau of statistics itself, the largest increase in two months since 1950. And, as proved by experience, an increase in wholesale prices always foreshadows a rise in retail prices, so that we must expect a record increase in the cost of living in the next few months.
We are in the very midst of inflation, and nothing can be more disastrous for a country than this. Indeed, inflation touches everybody, particularly those who are defenseless and who suffer, and especially those whose salaries do not rise as quickly as the cost of living. When prices go up, it is the white collar worker, the civil servant, widows and small wage earners who take the brunt of a lower standard of living.
The government has no overall program to fight this plague. There again, it wallows in confusion and uncertainty. With this financial crisis created by the government, and with soaring prices, there is more unemployment than in 1957. The unemployment situation remains very serious.
Not only was unemployment higher in 1958, but the number of workers was lower

than in 1957. As we were told yesterday, in mid-December there were 440,000 unemployed in Canada. In the province of Quebec, the situation is more serious than anywhere else, with the exception of the maritime provinces.
There are today, in the province of Quebec, 185,000 people looking for work. This is more than 8 per cent of the available labour force, or about one third of all the unemployed in Canada. In Montreal, 80,000 people are out of work. In Sorel, in Arvida, in the asbestos and textile industries that our hon. friends, particularly the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) were supposed to help out, conditions have never been worse.
Representatives of the textile industries complained about it yesterday, at a meeting held in Ottawa. Consequently I have no hesitation in saying that, with respect to unemployment and to the financial situation, the government has no comprehensive plan to cure the evil. Besides, the speech from the throne is non-committal and announces no new measure to cope with the situation.
We no longer hear about the great billion-dollar public works program, so often mentioned during the last elections. We hear, instead, of the winter program of assistance to municipalities.
This idea, Mr. Speaker, is not new. Indeed, the Liberals suggested it during the last election campaign, and even proposed it, as did the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) during the parliamentary session. We tried, by all possible means, to convince the government to put into force this policy. We did not succeed at the time, but the government finally decided to accept our proposal, but unfortunately its decision came too late. The plan was announced too late to improve the lot of those who suffer in these winter months. It was put forward in late October, at the very time when the Prime Minister was about to leave on his trip around the world.
Actually it was then too late for municipalities to plan such works, which should have started by early November if they were to have any effect in relieving seasonal unemployment.
Besides, the program put forth by the government is much too restrictive to deal with the problem. On December 24, 1958, the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) announced that, between December 1 and April 30, his program would cost the federal

government $3,900,000. Will you please tell me, Mr. Speaker, what good an outlay of $3,900,000 can possibly be in helping the country's 440,000 unemployed? The hon. minister admitted that at the time the province of Quebec had submitted no project in connection with this winter works program.
This winter works program for municipalities can therefore be of absolutely no use to the province of Quebec, because so far she did not take advantage of it, although at this time 185,000 persons are seeking jobs. Yet in Montreal, on March 20 last, the Minister of Labour did not hesitate to forecast that unemployment would have vanished by mid-June.
What about the oft-repeated words of the right hon. Prime Minister to the effect that no one would suffer from unemployment on account of him? Will he take offence if I tell him that, at the present time, there are 440,000 unemployed in Canada?
(Text):
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), in his intervention in the debate referred to the speech of the President of the United States. I wish he had gone on to deal further with that speech which the President made to congress, his usual state of the union speech, because if he had he would have noticed a part having to do with inflation. He would have noticed that the President said that because of the serious condition vis-a-vis inflation, because of the danger of future soaring prices and to keep the economy sound and expanding, he would present to congress at once certain proposals. He went on to list them. The first was a balanced budget for next year. This is advice which the Prime Minister might well follow.
Apparently the government, in dealing with unemployment, intends to follow the kind of approach that we on this side of the house have criticized, namely increased government expenditure. At least, this is what the Prime Minister led us to believe in his speech on Monday as recorded at page 65 of Hansard for January 19, 1959. He said:
But I believe the people of Canada as a whole want us to make the necessary expenditures to meet the spectre of unemployment as it is found.
Well, you have listened to this statement by the Prime Minister. Now, contrast that with what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had to say in Toronto in his famous speech on January 5. After going on to say
The Address-Mr. Chevrier that the expenses of government were high; that the line must be held; that expenditures must be paid; that a high standard of living and of social services and the like must be maintained, he said this, and I quote:
Nevertheless the treasury board in its current review of estimates is, I assure you, applying a firm hand to controllable expenditures.
On the one hand, the Minister of Finance is saying he is going to hold the line, but the Prime Minister is saying, when circumstances warrant it, there will be no hesitation about additional public expenditures. There is another example of contradiction and confusion.
It is equally evident that in following that object to fight unemployment, the government, as in so many other fields, lacks imagination in finding new and useful projects to initiate. When we speak in this house we are interrupted by ministers and others who say, well, what are your proposals; what have you got to offer? Even if we do not agree fundamentally with the government's approach, as was made clear by my leader the other day, I should like at this juncture to make some suggestions to the government. Unemployment, as I said earlier, is more serious in the province of Quebec and in the city of Montreal than in any other part of Canada with the exception of the Atlantic provinces. I am going to make three suggestions and I hope that they will receive serious consideration.
The first is for the immediate appointment of a board of engineers for the purpose of studying and reporting upon the economic advantages of linking the St. Lawrence river with the port of New York via the Richelieu river, lake Champlain and the Hudson river. This matter was taken up in the house and is contained in a resolution by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin). It is a problem which is not new. Representations have already been made to the government. This matter was referred in 1937 to the international joint commission. I hold in my hand a copy of the report which was made at that time, and in effect it states this: As soon as the St. Lawrence seaway has been completed this matter of the Champlain-Richelieu canal should be given consideration by the international commission.
I wish I had time to go into the matter more fully. All I can say at this time is this: If it were given consideration and put into effect by a recommendation, of course following a report of a board of engineers, it would put to work thousands of people in an area where work is required.
The second suggestion I have to make has to do with the joint development of power

The Address-Mr. Chevrier and navigation in the Lachine section of the river. I will be told at once that this is purely a provincial matter. This is true to some extent, save that in 1947 a board of engineers appointed by the government reported that navigation and power production in the Lachine section was feasible and that if it were put into effect it would bring about greater savings in power development in the Montreal area. It is quite clear that if the recommendations contained in this report were given effect, thousands of people could be put to work.
All we have to do is see what happened in the international section of the river in so far as the St. Lawrence seaway was concerned where at least half if not more of the 25,000 men employed on that project were put to work on power development. If it were possible for the government, which is extremely friendly I understand with the government of Mr. Duplessis in the province of Quebec, to make the requisite representations and to convince him-incidentally it has already been announced by a commissioner of Quebec Hydro-that this is a project which should be undertaken without delay, as I am sure he himself is convinced, it would be a great boon to the area of Montreal.
Finally, I suggest the construction of a new bridge linking Montreal and the south shore downstream from the Jacques Cartier bridge. I am sure, from what I know of the traffic conditions, that there is no member in this house, no matter on what side of the house he sits, who would not be in favour of the construction of such a bridge. As I said earlier, I wish I had more time to deal with these three matters, but unfortunately 1 must go on.

speechtext:
If the hon. member had listened to what I said he would find that most of these projects are self-liquidating. The bridge is self-liquidating, the power project is self-liquidating and the Champlain-Richelieu project would be self-liquidating if tolls were to be charged.
I should like to commend the government for recommending to parliament the establishment of the Canada-United States interparliamentary group. I believe that that is a useful


body. The Canadian section was enthusiastically received in the United States and the speakers of both houses, I have no hesitation in saying, handled the meetings with tact and diplomacy. I should like to warn the Prime Minister, however, that he should not overstate the case, as he did the other day because, after all, this is only one of many such committees and it is hard to say how much will be accomplished by it. A large number of questions were mentioned for discussion- they did not come up for discussion, but a large number were listed for discussion-and of all these questions two seemed to stand out above all the others. The first was defence, and the next was trade.
On the question of defence I should like to say this: we are told that defence must be continental; we are told that defence must be arranged jointly with our friends in the United States, and to that there can be no objection. But defence, I think, is a two-way street. It must be joint not only from the viewpoint of the military aspect but also from the viewpoint of the economic and industrial aspect. What I want to suggest to the government in this respect is the revival of the Hyde Park agreement. This agreement was established in 1941. It was a declaration between the Right Hon. Mr. King and Mr. Roosevelt and it was established for two purposes, the first of which was to relieve the substantial adverse balance of trade which had developed between Canada and the United States at the time and next to make sure that no useless defence production facilities would be produced in either country. The circumstances today are exactly the same as they were then, and it seems to me that the time has come for a revival of the Hyde Park agreement or something akin thereto.
It is all very well for us to be told that there should be joint defence between the two countries, but how can it be joint if on the one hand we are refused the entry of our exports such as oil, lead and zinc. I notice that there is something in the speech from the throne having to do with this question, but that is not enough. I think there has to be far more than that and I think there should be a determined effort by the government to make sure that Canadian companies have the opportunity to bid in the United States market with regard to defence orders. There is very little in the way of defence orders that cannot be manufactured in Canada by our own industry.
I could take as an example the CF-105, and while I know of the difficulties in the way I will suggest that in view of the statements made by Air Vice Marshal Slemon and General Partridge it is an efficient manned interceptor in the light of the requirements for

which it was produced. It would seem to me that this would be a good place at which to start by selling this aircraft to the United States. That is just one example. There are hundreds of other things which could be produced in Canada and which could be sold in the United States.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow a question, because I know he took a considerable interest in the revival of the Hyde Park agreement on the occasion of this meeting in August, or so I am informed. Did he find any reaction favourable to the CF-105 being purchased by the United States during his visit to Washington in August?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
I did not discuss the purchase of the CF-105, but I did discuss the revival of the Hyde Park agreement and while I am precluded from mentioning names it was clearly stated to me by one member of the group that there was no reason why Canadian manufacturers should not be allowed to sell their products on the United States market.
Now I want to say a word about the dispute which arose sometime ago between the radio and television producers in Montreal and the C.B.C. which has caused the interruption of the normal operations of the whole French network during the last three weeks and which may destroy the good relationship which existed between the C.B.C. and its employees. This is a matter of deep concern, not only for the parties immediately involved in the dispute but also for all Canadians interested in an efficient broadcasting system in our country. And yet the government has done nothing to help the two parties come to a satisfactory agreement.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) stated in the house last Friday that he had taken no action whatsoever with respect to this strike, but then he went on to say that the strike was entirely illegal and, in his own words, that "rationality apparently is one thing that has been somewhat lacking in the situation." The minister, as he said, has done nothing to settle the dispute, and the words he used last Friday to describe the situation will not be useful in bringing about a satisfactory solution.
On the same day, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) said he was not prepared to intervene in the dispute, adding that the parties were seeking to short-cut or ignore the provisions of the legislation designed for the final disposition of disputes dealing with representation, and he implied that he could not intervene under section 56 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act because that section provided for the appointment of a commissioner of inquiry into labour disputes on the basis of a collective agreement.
The Address-Mr. Chevrier I say to the house and to the minister that this very narrow interpretation is not compatible with the wording of the act. Section 56, subsection 1, reads as follows:
The minister may either upon application or of his own initiative, where he deems it expedient, make or cause to be made any inquiries he thinks fit regarding industrial matters, and may do such things as seem calculated to maintain or secure industrial peace and to promote conditions favourable to settlement of disputes.
Our legislation provides, of course, for a procedure of certification by the labour relations board. However, that procedure is not compulsory. Representation can still be a matter of negotiation between parties. When it is so negotiated and when such negotiations lead to a dispute, then the minister can intervene and he should do so in major conflicts such as the present one. The failure of the minister to act in this case is another example of fumbling and uncertainty on the part of the government.
The proposal made by the C.B.C. on January 16 was to the effect that the corporation was prepared to recognize the producers association and to discuss with it general working conditions, provided that if at any time there was disagreement between the two parties the dispute would be submitted for final decision to an arbitrator who would be the president of the corporation. This proposal was certainly unacceptable to the producers and would have put the president of the C.B.C. in a most embarrassing position where he would have been at the same time judge and employer.
According to press reports, the producers submitted another proposal to the C.B.C. which seemed far more reasonable. That proposal has now been refused by the C.B.C. which according to a news bulletin this morning has issued an ultimatum to its employees to return to work on Thursday of this week or else lose their jobs.
Mr. Speaker, this dispute has been allowed to go on far too long. Is the Minister of Labour going to sit idly by and allow the C.B.C. to put this ultimatum into effect? If this strike were in the minister's constituency would he allow the situation to develop as it has? If it were in his constituency would he allow his colleague the Minister of National Revenue to rise and say that the strike is illegal? I doubt very much that he would.
If the C.B.C. is allowed to implement its ultimatum not only the producers are in danger of losing their jobs but the French network will lose highly qualified personnel, which cannot adequately be replaced at this time and the public, which foots the bill, is the one that in the last analysis will suffer. It is the clear responsibility not only under

The Address-Mr. Chevrier moral law but under the statute, subsection 1 of section 56 which I have just quoted, for the minister to intervene and to do his utmost to bring about a settlement of this dispute.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, in closing I should like to touch upon another subject. Recently, two ministers of the Right Hon. Mr. Diefenbaker's government, speaking of our national anthem, said that Canada's national anthem is God Save the Queen, and that it is ridiculous to think otherwise. O Canada, they said, was a pretty song, but does not enjoy the status of a national anthem.
There we have two ministers who, in my opinion, never understood either the word or the spirit of confederation, two ministers who never understood the true Canadian spirit. And their recent statements are much more calculated to split than to unite this country. Yet when either of them goes abroad, as often as does the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith), to represent Canada, it is not God Save the Queen, but indeed O Canada that is sung at official meetings.
Under the Liberal government this matter was gone into, and the former prime minister, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent himself, definitely stated the position. In reply to a question from the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asking whether, in fact, God Save the Queen was Canada's national anthem, Mr. St. Laurent replied that God Save the Queen had never been adopted either by the Canadian parliament or by resolution or by proclamation as a national anthem, and that, for many Canadians, O Canada was considered as the national anthem.
It is therefore not for two cabinet ministers of the present government to tell us that God Save the Queen is Canada's national anthem.
For my part, I shall always respect God Save the Queen, and will sing it in chorus with other Canadians when the occasion offers, recognizing it as the royal anthem. But in my estimation, and in the judgment, I am sure, of many Canadian citizens, the national anthem of this country remains O Canada.
In closing my observations, I should like to recall the words of Sir George Etienne Cartier, a great Conservative, but first and foremost a great Canadian.

In the course of the press conference in which I was engaged there was one doublebarrelled question which the Leader of the Opposition mentioned on Monday and of which he did not approve. Here it is verbatim. He gave it; I will give it. This is the way it was phrased:
Now, which of these two, unemployment or inflation, do you regard as being the greatest threat to our economy during 1959?
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) put this question to the Leader of the Opposition, the Leader of the Opposition quibbled and evaded and said, "Of course, it is quite ridiculous to make that kind of mathematical comparison." I gave a much more forthright answer and I am going to give it in full here today. I said this:
I don't think either will be a threat to our economy in 1959. I think 1959 is going to be a good year, and so it says in the document ''The Year-end Review" which came out just at the end of December, because the recession which plagued us and the United States, starting in 1957, has pretty well come to an end. We have made a recovery from that, and 1959, with the way things are going, should be a good year for us. More people wili be employed and conditions generally will be better.
The Leader of the Opposition did not read out those words of mine which would have been helpful to him. Then, the members of the press conference came back to the question of inflation later on and I will indicate to my hon. friend that there is no confusion in the minds of the members of the party on this side of the house. Did I understand you to say you do not think inflation is a threat in 1959?

I replied:
I think the Minister of Finance dealt with this subject in a speech yesterday in Toronto. Have you got that in front of you? You people are very well briefed. It was praised so much I thought he was enthusiastic about it. The Minister of Finance said this:
I do not deplore the current evidence of concern over inflation. On the contrary, I think it is a healthy sign that people are showing concern for the preservation of the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar. That degree of public concern will, I trust, assist governments and others in grappling with the problem. I am concerned, however, that the discussion of this subject should be realistic and balanced. The danger of inflation exists, as it has existed for the last 20 years. We will not, however, overcome it by exaggerating it beyond all recognition.
Therefore, I say unemployment and inflation are not threats in the sense that the Canadian economy is in danger of collapse from these two problems. They are serious matters that have to be dealt with courageously and vigorously and that is what this government is doing.
The greatest threat to Canada's economy is the attitude of mind displayed on Monday by the Leader of the Opposition. Talking blue ruin, spreading gloom and despondency, arousing fear in the minds of our people, that is the method by which progress can be retarded, that is the method by which confidence can be destroyed, that is the


method by which Canada's name can be smeared and doubt and uncertainty aroused in the minds of foreign observers.

speechtext: May I ask a question? Did the hon. gentleman have that view when he and his colleagues made those gloomy speeches about unemployment in 1955?
