I am much more an optimist than my friend, formerly from Manitoba. He has lost some of that western spirit and optimism about life. He is fogbound, I think. I was saying, how typical of the Liberal party. That is the age-old weakness of the Liberals, little Canadianism, no breadth of vision, no inspirational leadership; just expediency, carping criticism and small-mindedness. No wonder the people of Canada revolted and by the peaceful method of the ballot swept out of office these men of little vision.
Canadians are proud of their country, inspired by the prospects of a glorious future, eager for advancement and development and ready to follow inspiring leadership.
The leader of the Liberal party is engaged with his brain trust in a task of rebuilding a bomb-shattered party. I suggest to him that he examine the history of his party over the years. He will find that the greatest weakness of the Liberal party from confederation to the present time has been its inability to raise its eyes from the ground and see the far horizon.
Had the Canadian people placed their confidence in the Liberal party from 1867 to 1896 there would have been no transcontinental railway to link the provinces together; British Columbia would not have entered confederation, as was pointed out so forcefully yesterday by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., (Mr. McPhillips); the prairie west would have been handed over to United States railways; Canada would have failed to achieve her destiny.
The narrow point of view of the Liberal party was demonstrated by the leader of that party during the spring election campaign. His reaction to the Conservative policy of developing the Canadian northland, a policy so brilliantly depicted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), a policy being so ably developed by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) was ridiculed by the Leader of the Opposition. In his words you can see the attitude of the Liberal party toward development. This is what he said as reported in the Montreal Star of March 1. These are his very words:
They are going to build a highway in the Arctic, beginning at one igloo and ending at another.
The same attitude of mind has characterized the Liberal party with regard to the

The Address-Mr. Churchill
commonwealth. "Play down the commonwealth" has been the Liberal slogan for 40 years. In his speech on Monday the Leader of the Opposition once again played down the commonwealth. Here are his words, as reported at page 44 of Hansard, with regard to the commonwealth conference held at Montreal in September last:
There was nothing unique about it in its assembling or its results.
I was not surprised at his statement, for a few years ago I examined the record of the hon. member with regard to the commonwealth. I searched Hansard for his comments and I read his words. It was an unrewarding experience. I then recorded my findings, and as he has been quoting from some of my speeches I will quote from some of them too just for the record and for the advice they may offer to the Leader of the Opposition. This is what I said on November 27, 1956, as found at page 101 of Hansard. I was speaking then of the person who was then secretary of state for external affairs, the present Leader of the Opposition, and this is what I said:
I wish he would speak more frequently on the commonwealth in the House of Commons. I have examined the number of times the Secretary of State for External Affairs has dealt with the British commonwealth of nations in the House of Commons. He has been goaded into making statements by people mentioning the subject here or asking him questions: but he has not, certainly in recent years himself made a speech on the British commonwealth of nations.
Then, on January 22, 1957, I was speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I hope the last speech from the throne that will be issued by the Liberal party certainly for a generation. In that throne speech were these words:
My ministers remain convinced of the need to maintain the basic unity of the commonwealth-
As found at page 524 of Hansard for January 22, 1957, I said:
This is indeed an unusual sentence. No such reference to the commonwealth appears in any speech from the throne from 1949 to the present time. Here and there in the preceding sessions casual reference was made to the commonwealth in those years in which commonwealth conferences were being held but this is the first occasion since 1949 on which the commonwealth has received special attention in the speech from the throne.
I suggested that the phraseology should have been as follows:
My ministers, and particularly the minister of external affairs, have suddenly discovered the British commonwealth of nations. Heretofore they have been only half conscious of its existence and have made little or no effort to maintain the basic unity of the commonwealth or even mention the subject.
The commonwealth conference held at Montreal was far from being just one among many. It was a unique conference. It was the 66968-9-11
first full-scale commonwealth conference on trade and economic problems held since 1932. It was the largest commonwealth conference ever held and one of the largest international conferences held in Canada. It was unique in scale, in the coverage of trade and economic policy matters that were dealt with, in the intensive preparations preceding it, in the number of ministers and senior officials attending from each government and in the scope and far-reaching nature of its results. It not only strengthened trade and economic ties among the commonwealth countries but it gave new impetus to multilateral policies on a world-wide basis. Many of the matters on which agreement was reached at the Montreal conference are now being followed up in broader world-wide forums such as the international monetary fund and the GATT.
This commonwealth conference came about as a result of Conservative party policy expressed repeatedly down through the years, and no one has expressed that policy more consistently or more vigorously than the Prime Minister. It was his suggestion that such a conference be held. The groundwork was laid for the conference at Mont Trem-blant a year earlier when the finance and trade ministers of the commonwealth assembled.
The results have been excellent. A basis has been laid for enlarging commonwealth trade and a basis laid for strengthening the commonwealth. The Prime Minister's recent visit to most of the member countries of the commonwealth has been just one more piece of evidence of the importance that the government places on this association of free and independent nations, and one more instance of the inspiring leadership of our Prime Minister.
What the Liberal party has never realized and does not now recognize is that Canada's status in international affairs owes much to her membership within the commonwealth. Nor does the Liberal party see that by the turn of this century Canada will occupy a position of even greater importance within the commonwealth and that that free association of nations, united under the crown and operating under the parliamentary system, will be an even stronger force for the maintenance of the freedom of mankind.
The Leader of the Opposition's flippant attitude towards the commonwealth is paralleled by his equally flippant attitude towards Canadian-United States relations.

The fumbling and bumbling of the Liberal party over the years with the United States has been part of the multitudinous errors of the former government that we have been successfully overcoming.
Thanks again to the leadership of the Prime Minister, Canada has made another advance in international affairs and relations between our country and the United States are on a better footing than they have ever been before. The Prime Minister faced up to the issue with courage in his speech at Dartmouth over a year ago. He has established the friendliest relationship with United States leaders. He has given encouragement to the meetings of cabinet ministers with the United States administration. Under his direction the latest development has been a committee of both houses to confer with representatives of the United States senate and house of representatives. At no time in our history has there been a better understanding by the people of the United States of the Canadian position. Never before has there been as wide a coverage of Canadian affairs in United States papers.
The timorous attitude of mind, so typical of the Liberal party, was due to the policy pursued by the Leader of the Opposition when he was secretary of state for external affairs. In those years he was tip-toeing through the tulips, afraid to say boo to a goose, and during the last two years he and his colleagues have attempted to portray the Conservative party as being anti-American. I well recall that when we took office 18 months ago the official Ottawa attitude was: Be careful what you say to the Americans, they might take offence. Members of the Liberal party have endeavoured to convey that type of fear ever since.
The Leader of the Opposition made some remarks concerning a speech I delivered in Chicago some time ago, and he thought that this was an expression of opinion at which he might cast some ridicule. I was referring, and the audience in Chicago understood this
(Mr. Martin (Essex East).]
very well, to the type of remarks made by our political opponents. As a result of this attitude during the last two years the impression created in the United States was that Canada was turning anti-American.
I had the good fortune to speak to the economic club in New York earlier. I am sorry that the Leader of the Opposition^ did not read my speech there and quote from it. The executive director of the economic club of New York came here twice to confer with me with regard to the nature of the speech I might make there. He said, "The impression that has been created in the United States"-it could only have been created by our political opponents-"is that your new government is opposed to Americans." He said, "Come on down and tell us about the things that are bothering you in Canada." I said, "All right, I will speak about the irritants in Canadian-United States relations", and I did. Of course, I was advised that I would be considered antiAmerican so I took the audience in New York into my confidence. I told them I had been advised by certain people that if I spoke in this fashion I would be considered anti-American.
They just loved it. After the conclusion of the speech the chairman said, "If this is anti-Americanism, give us more of it". I am sorry I have not the time in which to give some quotation from that speech I made in New York. I followed a somewhat similar line in a similar speech made in Chicago. The Americans like straightforward talk. They understand Canadians and we understand them. They are prepared to consider the difficulties that arise normally in the trading relations between our two countries.
The Leader of the Opposition then went on to talk about our trade with the United States and he again passed the remarks that he has made so often with regard to what he has called a policy of diversion of trade. Our policy has been an expansion of trade. Over the years we have taken the stand that it has been wrong to have all of our trade with the United States of America; that our trade should be world-wide; that if our trade is concentrated with one country, then we are likely to suffer when that country has a set-back or perhaps has a change of opinion with regard to some of the things that enter it. When there has been over the years a serious imbalance in our trade with one country, it is only prudence to attempt to expand your trade elsewhere in the world. That is exactly what we have done and we have had success in doing it.

Hon. members on the other side, members of the Liberal party, spoke words of derision with regard to the trade mission which visited the United Kingdom a little over a year ago. It was so successful that, of course, they had to find fault with it; and the long term results of that trade mission are being felt now in Canada. That was just one move in the general direction and following the general policy of expanding our trade throughout the world. After all, Canada is a trading nation. It is the fourth largest trading nation in the world. About one out of every five Canadians is dependent upon our export trade.
The Leader of the Opposition attempted to show that our export trade and our trade generally had declined. Let me put this on the record. On the basis of figures available to date-that is from the dominion bureau of statistics-world trade declined by approximately 7 per cent in 1958 and United States industrial production was also appreciably lower. The fact that Canada's exports were maintained in the face of these adverse conditions is a reflection not of weakness but of the underlying strength in Canada's present trade position.
In this connection a comparison of current trends with those in 1954 is relevant. The 1954 recession in the United States was milder than the recent one and European economies had continued to expand. Nevertheless, Canada's exports in physical volume terms declined three per cent between 1953 and 1954. In short, our exports have faired better in 1958 despite a weaker international situation. Our exports have been equal in 1958 to those in 1957 which established a record.
The Leader of the Opposition and his colleague talk about trade but they do not get down to the basic facts or give us the information which is required in connection with these matters so that the people can form a fair comparison. The Leader of the Opposition also talked about our wheat exports and once again, as he has done in the past, he mentioned the fact that they had exceeded those of the previous year. Then, of course, he threw in a gibe about this being due to gifts and long term loans under the Colombo plan. I hope the Leader of the Opposition was not attempting to give the impression that he is opposed to making gifts of surplus food to hungry people within the commonwealth but that is the impression that he is creating by these remarks.

In rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I first want to congratulate the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply for their contributions. They both did exceedingly well. I realize, however, that the speech from the throne was not of their making. In my opinion there is nothing in the speech from the throne to correct the ills that beset us in this country where we have so many natural resources. Traditionally, these hon. members made reference to their own constituencies and this was very interesting. I should like to follow their example and make some reference to my own constituency of Welland.
We have fine people living in the constituency of Welland. Anglo-Saxon people comprise the majority of our population, but during the last generation or so we have had a great influx of French-speaking Canadians as well as people from southern and western Europe. These people live in complete harmony, and they and their descendants are making a fine contribution to our Canadian

way of life. There is no other part of Canada that I would rather represent than the constituency of Welland.
Our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) graced Welland with a visit last March during his election tour. No one took the trouble to invite me to that meeting but I learned what occurred there. I can assure the Prime Minister that if he will come back now, he will have an even larger meeting. Some of the people who attended the last meeting said they would provide him with a theme song, "Oh, Promise Me". The meeting the Prime Minister held in Welland was, in part at least, composed of a captive audience because school children were brought in by the bus load from schools in the surrounding school areas. Then, too, many people arrived at the meeting at no cost to themselves because a canvass had been made and car drivers were paid $5 and $10 to deliver loads of people to that meeting.
There were many people, however, who attended the meeting without any urging. I refer now to the unemployed and the fruit and vegetable growers. What they heard from the Prime Minister in the way of promises must have been music to their ears. According to the press, he promised the unemployed that no one would suffer as a result of unemployment as long as he was Prime Minister of Canada. He went even further than that, and this was afterwards echoed on television by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) when he said that the unemployment would be pretty well cleared up by mid-summer. Mid-summer has come and gone and many of these same men and women are still unemployed. Their numbers have greatly increased in the Welland area.
At the time of the June election when this government came into power, we had comparatively few unemployed. When the Prime Minister was in Welland the number stood at about 2,400. Today it is difficult to ascertain the exact number. I am told it is in the neighbourhood of 4,000. These figures used to be published, but they are not published any longer. The reeve of one municipality told me that the relief rolls were up by about 400 per cent over those of a year ago. In the practice of medicine I meet and treat many of the unemployed. I know that they want work and not the dole. Many of them have purchased homes, furniture and the other necessities of life. They have had to go into debt and they cannot meet their obligations. Surely this government should soon realize that it does not help the peace of mind of the unemployed to be told that while unemployment is greater this winter it is not increasing as greatly percentage-wise. Last night I believe the Minister of Finance, speaking in the Chateau
The Address-Mr. McMillan Laurier, used the word "proportion", and said that the proportion of increase of unemployed was not as great.
When a man is out of work, just getting a mere subsistance for himself and his family, these vague percentage quotations by the government do nothing to lighten his burden. I feel heartily sorry for the unemployed and our government is doing nothing to provide work for the younger people coming into the labour market. The new federal-provincial scheme to help municipalities provide work for the unemployed by helping to provide new projects for the municipalities is of little use. It is too little and too late.
The St. Catharines Standard for example, a few days ago had an article which said that not one man hour of work had been provided in that city for the unemployed by this scheme. Also, I have a letter here from the city of Welland claiming that the help provided under this scheme is too restricted. This was written to me by the city clerk of Welland, and he says that the council and corporation of Welland at its meeting on January 6, 1959, viewed with alarm the narrow limits of unemployment assistance and work projects available to the smaller cities in the province of Ontario. I know that this scheme is of little help in the towns and smaller cities. I am not familiar with how the scheme might work out in the larger cities, but I fail to see that it can be of any great help, particularly since I have seen the figure given out by the Department of Labour. Canada cannot afford to have so many people unemployed and non-productive. There is nothing which breaks the spirit and morale of a person more than idleness. Canadians deserve the right to work.
At the meeting in Welland the Prime Minister also dwelt on the poor returns received by fruit and vegetable growers for their products. I agree with the Prime Minister that they should have had a greater share of the national income. But what has happened since this government came to power? Many of these fruit and vegetable growers tell me that their costs have risen and their returns for 1958 in respect of their crops have been the worse since before the war. The Prime Minister made a very emotional appeal. There was a fine old lady at that meeting who came from a farm community. She wept because she said she had never heard a man speak with such sympathy for the farmers as did the Prime Minister that day. The price of asparagus was very much to the fore.
Spring was coming on, and these producers were very much concerned about the price. In the year before, under the Liberal government, the price had fallen from 23 cents

The Address-Mr. McMillan to 22 cents and in some cases to 21-|- cents. Now what has happened? The present government set the floor at 18 cents under which they placed a three cent deficiency payment, and asparagus has never since that time sold above 15 cents in Ontario and 14 cents in British Columbia. In the province of Ontario the government paid a deficiency payment of three cents a pound so that the producer in Ontario got 18 cents and the producer in British Columbia received 17 cents.
As for peaches, the floor price was set at $83 a ton which is the lowest price received by the peach growers for grade A peaches since before the war. I understand that the government has not yet settled with the growers for this year. We understand that cherries could not be all sold and that much of the crop rotted on the trees. The cold storage plants took all they could but according to the last information I received before Christmas the farmers had not been paid for this fruit put into cold storage. There is one big chain store in the Niagara district which was selling American table corn when our corn was ripe. You could stand in the store and look out the window and see the farmers harvesting their corn in the adjoining fields.
I think that our unemployment and our depressed economy are in a considerable part due to the trade and fiscal policies of this government. I will give some examples of each. Hon. members will recall that in June of 1957 our economy was good. In fact, it was so good that the Prime Minister said he could divert 15 per cent of trade from the United States to Great Britain. Hon. members will also recall that about the same time, or shortly afterwards, the United States accommodated the Prime Minister by cutting off 15 per cent of our oil imports into the northwestern United States. Then, in December of 1957, this government sent a buying mission to Britain; they were to buy and not to sell Canadian products and this was done at a time when unemployment in Britain was very low and when in Canada we had plenty. We got a report from that buying mission. This report was printed in Toronto and not by the queen's printer. Oddly enough, that report refers to nothing that was bought. It reads something like the social column of a woman's page in a newspaper. It says whom the delegation visited, by whom they were received, how they were entertained, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) joined the group, when he left it and when he rejoined it.
The only inkling I received that a big trade switch was on was in a Port Colborne newspaper. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was there, according to the paper,

and he announced that the government intended to switch even more trade from the United States to Britain than it had already done. I can thank the hon. minister for helping to elect me because by that time our unemployment in the Welland area had increased from practically nothing to about 2,400. I argued that if the big switch had helped produce that many it was surely time to call a halt to that type of cause of unemployment.
This evening I heard the minister refer to the fact that we would in time see the long term result of this attempt to switch trade to Britain. I do not know anything about the long term result; I am giving one of the short term results. I have always been greatly interested in Canada's effort to promote trade with Britain. Since our trade with the United States has been cut by about 15 per cent I wondered why our trade with Britain had not been increased. Following our buying mission to Britain, however, our imports went down by 7.6 per cent in the third quarter of 1958 and by about 1 per cent for the first nine months of 1958.
It appears to me that before our government meets in conference with the United States or even with members of the commonwealth it always seems to give them a slap in the face first. We all recall the first conference of our four ministers with their opposite numbers in the United States when secretary of commerce, Sinclair Weeks, said to reporters: "we fixed them." I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) got another explanation to mean that he meant: "We fixed them up". But the newspaper accounts, even in the Toronto Globe and Mail at that time talked about the brush-off our ministers received in Washington.
The United States is our best customer, and living along the border as I do I have an opportunity to see many of the Buffalo and Niagara Falls newspapers, among others, which circulate in our area. I have had the opportunity to read them over the years. Some have said quite openly that if the Canadian Prime Minister and his followers acted as some of them were talking, the election foreboded a difficult period in trade and other relations between the United States and Canada. One paper in my area-a paper that supports this government-went so far as to say it would not be surprised if incidents occurred between Canadians and Americans living in the Niagara district.
The United States press referred to the diversion of trade proposed by this government and later on in one or two dispatches from Ottawa it was stated that Canadian raw

materials such as iron ore would be processed in Canadian plants and not shipped south of the border to give jobs to people in the United States. I think it is fine to process all the raw materials we can but I could not conceive of a worse preparation for a conference with our United States friends.
How about the commonwealth conference itself? We have had two of them, first the Mont Tremblant conference and latterly the Montreal conference. The preparation for the Montreal conference involved an added tariff, as hon. members will recall, placed on British woollens, a procedure of this government that certainly did not go unnoticed by the British government.
I have in my hand a copy of Hansard, of the British House of Commons of December 2, 1958 when the government of that country debated commonwealth affairs and I shall quote extracts from the speeches of a Conservative member, a Labour member and a Liberal member. I should like to ask some of the members of the Conservative party in this house to read what Sir Albert Braith-waite said about the Montreal conference. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) said that the commonwealth conference was unique. We shall see how unique it was. These are the remarks of Sir Albert Braithwaite the Conservative member for Harrow West:
First of all, I should like to pay tribute to the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the president of the board of trade for the brilliance which they displayed in leading our own delegation to the Montreal conference. Reading between the lines, it seems to me that what they did there literally saved the conference from being almost a stalemate. They infused some life into it. At the same time I am not satisfied that the conference report is by any means a document upon which to rebuild and revitalize the British commonwealth of nations. Its implications are narrow. It is phlegmatic. It is not precise enough in its conclusions, and it gives no real, positive direction on how even those conclusions will be carried out.
I wanted something much more vital to lead our commonwealth affairs than a lot of pious platitudes. Many people have said a great many things about how we should develop the commonwealth but there has been a remarkable absence of action since the Montreal conference took place. The Canadian Prime Minister came over here and made great speeches on what should be done, but I have seen no real reflection in deeds implementing the words which he uttered.

As we say, a peculiar year; a year in which our economy found itself very much out of balance, if not indeed out of control. Sweeping changes are obviously in order from top to bottom of our economic life; and this will require strong leadership. We have a right to expect, and demand, such leadership during 1959 from those in a position to provide it.
I hope the government can provide it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before embarking on a few comments I should like to add my voice to the congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Like previous speakers, I was very impressed with the speeches that the hon. member for Pro-vencher and the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet made, and I congratulate them.
I was surprised, Mr. Speaker, and continue to be surprised that we should have heard so much gloom, doom and criticism from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and now from his followers. I was surprised because it is quite obvious that he is still far removed from the grass roots in the country. You will remember that when he became leader of the party he said that it was time

The Address-Miss Aitken that the Liberals got away from the brass and back to the grass. I was surprised to hear all this gloom and doom because, as I think most of us will agree, one would have thought that after our four-month recess the Leader of the Opposition would have a better idea of what the people of Canada, the grass roots, are really thinking.
Personally, I am extremely gratified at the political consciousness of the people, certainly those in my constituency of York-Humber, and I am grateful for their awareness of the problems that face us all in Canada. I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has played a major role in sparking the interest of the people in our national welfare. He has the great gift of getting close to the people, of inspiring belief

in him and in his honesty, courage and deep sense of responsibility.
On the other hand, nothing will convince me that the Leader of the Opposition, in his pitiful pessimism, is speaking for the people of Canada, the grass roots of Canada. He may have been speaking for the sadly decimated Liberal party but certainly not for the people of Canada. There are three or four items I should like to speak about with reference to the speech from the throne. Shall I go ahead or shall I call it six o'clock?
